texts.954a84d3c506: Objective for processing: To determine whether up to 15 years, aneurysm related mortality is higher after endovascular aortic repair than after open repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). Follow up to 10 years of patients enrolled in the UK EVAR 1 trial (NEJM 362: 1863-1871) has illustrated the problems associated with late secondary EVAR sac rupture. These late secondary EVAR sac ruptures occur at a low but persistent rate and are fatal in two thirds of cases. Therefore the applicant seeks to assess whether the late outcome after endovascular loses any early advantages in mortality than those after open repair. This will inevitably affect cost effectiveness modelling and therefore the applicants also aims to inform the NHS of the best and most cost effective option (EVAR or open repair) for abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. For these purposes the applicant needs full and accurate data for hospital admissions for aneurysm related procedures to infer best data for AAA related mortality. Information received about aneurysm related complications will be matched to mortality information. The applicant receives mortality data for all patients enrolled in the EVAR trials under a separate medical research study with the HSCIC. The applicant will send the cohort for which HES data is being requested directly to the HSCIC via SEFT (NHS Number, Date of Birth, Gender and Study ID) as this is not retained by the HSCIC. Processing activities: The data will be processed on Imperial College Healthcare Trust computers at Charing Cross Hospital. Data will be at record level and any identifiable data removed (NHS Number & Date of Birth), before analysis by the applicants collaborating statistician. 1. The data will be cleaned and harmonised by Imperial researchers. 2. Key outputs, e.g. re-interventions (dates, type, etc.) will be matched with trial database through hospital number. 3. Anonymised version of expanded trial database (not at record level) sent to Statisticians in Cambridge. 4. Analyses will be carried out according to a predefined Statistical Analysis Plan. The programmes used are Stata and Excel. 5. Reporting and dissemination of results (medical journals, NIHR-HTA report) The amount of data requested is the minimum required to allow us to identify aneurysm related adverse events and mortality. All outputs will be aggregated and anonymised, and not used for any commercial purpose. The project is funded by NIHR, and Imperial College London is the trial sponsor. Although the funding from the NIHR is awarded to the university (Imperial College London), all staff working on the project are based on NHS Trust premises at Charing Cross Hospital and have honorary contracts with the NHS Trust. Staff under the honorary contract are obliged to comply with the terms of the IG Toolkit, and that the Trust is liable in event of any breach by those staff. Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): The 5 year and 10 year results were published in the New England Journal of Medicine. The applicant expects to publish the results from the current phase of follow-up (to 15 years) in the same journal or ones with a similar impact factor. The applicant is required by the funding body - the National Institute of Health Research (NIHR) Health Technology Appraisal (HTA) programme to produce a report which will be published by the NIHR. The EVAR trials have provided evidence upon which a number of detailed cost-effectiveness analyses have been undertaken, with the latest based on 10 years of follow-up. The proposed data collection will facilitate a within-trial cost-effectiveness analysis. The “within-trial” analysis will estimate mean total costs and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) of the randomised interventions based on individual patient data up to 15-years. The analysis will include the costs to the NHS of the initial aneurysm repairs (with open surgery or EVAR) and subsequent re-interventions. The HES records will enable us to identify aneurysm-related interventions and length of stay for each patient since 2009, regardless of whether this admission occurred at a trial hospital or not. These data, once cleaned and cross-referenced with the available data from the trials, will enable us to construct a complete picture of the follow-up for each patient. The application is for unfiltered data but for a limited number of HES fields have been requested (16 fields total.) The applicant will need this information to identify aneurysm related adverse events and mortality. Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): The choice of method of repair of the abdominal aortic aneurysm for future patients will be affected by the knowledge of the applicants late follow-up experience [From 2016]. At the end of the 10-year follow-up, the data available were used to assess the rate and factors associated with rupture after endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) or open repair (OR) of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) (Wyss 2010). Within this follow-up period 27 secondary ruptures of the excluded aneurysm occurred in patients with EVAR. These sac ruptures carried a mortality rate of 67% and it is possible that the early aneurysm related mortality benefit of EVAR is lost as a result of these late sac ruptures and death. If the trend observed at 10-years were to continue, after 15 years, open repair will have a lower aneurysm-related mortality than endovascular repair, even with every attempt taken to intervene to correct known causes of sac expansion to reduce the risk of secondary rupture in EVAR patients, The additional follow-up to 15 years including the information we will obtain from HES data will allow us to test this hypothesis. There are European guidelines which recommend at least one follow-up visit (including imaging) every 5 years for patients undergoing AAA repair using open or endovascular repair (ESVS). However in the applicants experience shows that this recommendation is not followed in current NHS practice. The HES data will allow us to evaluate the importance of careful long-term monitoring of patients after AAA repair even when repair has been carried out using the newer generation of endovascular devices. The National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) are currently in the process of setting up an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Guideline Committee. The results from the study will provide key data for guidelines to be produced relating to choice of method of repair (open v endovascular) and any recommendations for follow-up. References 1. Wyss, T.R., Brown, L.C., Powell, J.T., Greenhalgh, R.M. (2010). Rate and predictability of graft rupture after endovascular and open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair: data from the EVAR Trials. Ann Surg. 252: 805-812. Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg (2011) 41, S1-S58
